hints: Focus on the difference between a polar bond and a polar molecule, the shape decides if bond dipoles cancel.
Notice that every C-Cl bond is polar because Cl is more electronegative than C, while C-H is almost non-polar.
Look for the perfectly symmetrical tetrahedral molecule where all four identical dipoles pull equally and cancel to zero.
walkthrough:
**Recall what makes a dipole**

A molecule has an overall dipole if its polar bonds do not cancel out. Think of each polar bond as a little arrow pulling electrons toward the more electronegative atom.

Bond polarity: $\text{C}^{\delta+} - \text{Cl}^{\delta-}$

**Check the shape of these molecules**

All four molecules are tetrahedral based on carbon with four single bonds. The key question is symmetry. Are the four pulling groups identical or different?

Shape: tetrahedral, bond angle $\approx 109.5^{\circ}$

**See where dipoles cancel**

In $\text{CH}_3\text{Cl}$, $\text{CH}_2\text{Cl}_2$ and $\text{CHCl}_3$, the C-Cl and C-H pulls are different, so they cannot cancel and a net dipole remains. Only when all four bonds are identical C-Cl does the pull cancel perfectly in all directions.

Result: net dipole $= 0$ only for the symmetrical molecule

options.A: Incorrect. In CH3Cl there is one strongly polar C-Cl bond and three almost non-polar C-H bonds. The dipoles cannot cancel in this unsymmetrical arrangement, so the molecule is polar.
options.B: Incorrect. In CH2Cl2 there are two polar C-Cl bonds pulling one way and two C-H bonds the other way. The tetrahedral shape is unsymmetrical, so the bond dipoles add to give a net dipole.
options.C: Incorrect. In CHCl3 there are three polar C-Cl bonds and only one C-H bond. This is still unsymmetrical, so the three C-Cl dipoles do not cancel and the molecule stays polar.
options.D: Correct. In CCl4 all four bonds are identical polar C-Cl bonds arranged perfectly tetrahedrally. The four equal dipoles pull symmetrically in opposite directions and cancel exactly, so there is no overall dipole.
